analysis.one_liner: Bans most prerecorded robocalls and creates protections for phone subscribers' privacy.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in September 1991 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal to use auto-dialing machines to blast prerecorded sales calls to emergency lines at hospitals and fire departments, to cell phones and pagers, or to phone numbers on a national do-not-call list. It would have directed the Federal Communications Commission to design a system protecting home-phone subscribers from unwanted recorded sales pitches, and to require that any recorded sales call identify the business calling and hang up properly when the person called does. It would have let states keep tougher anti-robocall laws of their own.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people with home phones, who would get fewer intrusive recorded sales calls at no extra charge, and the staff of hospitals, fire departments, and police agencies whose emergency and pager lines would no longer be tied up by machine-dialed sales calls.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home phone subscribers and emergency services

how_it_helps.text: Bars prerecorded sales calls to emergency lines and pagers of hospitals, doctors' offices, health care facilities, fire departments, and law enforcement agencies, and to cellular and paging numbers.
Directs the FCC to create rules protecting home-phone subscribers from unwanted prerecorded sales calls, with no additional charge to subscribers.
Requires that any recorded sales call identify the business calling, give its phone number or address, and release the line within five seconds after the person called hangs up.

Lets states keep or pass tougher anti-robocall laws, noting in its findings that 21 states had already restricted auto-dialed sales calls but telemarketers could evade them by operating across state lines.
The bill's findings say auto-dialers can make 60 random sales calls an hour and that unrestricted telemarketing invades privacy and can endanger people waiting for emergency help.

analysis.who_pays: Telemarketing firms, which would face new equipment rules, calling bans, and compliance costs; the bill's own findings note the industry employed over 300,000 agents making 18 million calls a day, and some of those costs could fall on the businesses that hire telemarketers and, ultimately, on their customers.

drawbacks.text: The restrictions would fall on a large industry — the bill counts over 300,000 telemarketing agents making 18 million calls a day — and complying with new FCC technical standards and calling limits would cost telemarketing firms money, costs that could be passed on to the businesses whose products they sell.
The bill exempts calls made by tax-exempt nonprofits, so recorded fundraising calls would still reach people's homes.
Building and running a national database of restricted phone numbers would be a new administrative undertaking for the FCC on a short 240-day rulemaking deadline.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For anyone who has had dinner interrupted by a recorded sales pitch, or who has worried about an emergency line being busy because a machine was dialing sales calls, the benefits are direct and the costs are modest and borne mainly by the calling industry. The main honest objections are the compliance burden on telemarketing businesses and the exemption for nonprofit calls.

outcome.mechanism: A single senator introduced it, the Senate sent it to the Commerce Committee, the committee never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Arlen Specter introduced the bill on September 17, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
The committee took no further action recorded on the bill; its entire action history is introduction and referral.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill never advanced out of committee and never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telemarketing firms kept making auto-dialed prerecorded sales calls with no new federal restrictions from this bill; the phone subscribers who would have been protected got nothing from it.

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill to restrict prerecorded telephone sales calls.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled action on the bill; it died in committee without a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican senator sponsored it with no cosponsors of either party, and it never advanced far enough for any vote, so no party pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have banned auto-dialed prerecorded sales calls to protected numbers and required FCC standards for every recorded sales call, directly cutting the volume of calls an 18-million-calls-a-day industry could make. Its interest ran against subscribers' privacy, which was the point of the bill.

industries.industry: Businesses that advertise by recorded phone calls
industries.note: Their cheapest mass-sales channel would have been restricted and calls would have to disclose the caller and release lines promptly, raising the cost of reaching customers by phone.
